problem: LLM-based zero-shot navigation relies on a cascaded mapping, text translation and planning pipeline that suffers from depth and pose errors, heavy compute, and loses geometry in text. Direct VLM use cannot output 3D waypoints, and naive history encoding (captions or full image sequences) loses spatial information or is redundant.
motivation: Home robots need open-vocabulary object and instance search without precise maps. VLMs are good at multiple-choice discrimination over images but weak at continuous 3D reasoning, so navigation should be recast as best-view image selection. This requires plausible candidate views and a compact visual memory.
key_idea: Predict human-like future waypoints with a small learned model, render imagined views there with a novel view synthesis model, and let a frozen VLM pick the best view, with a sparse-to-dense keyframe memory supplying history.
insight: Ablation (Table 2) shows imagination alone lifts ObjectNav SR from 43.0 to 55.0 (oracle views), Where2Imagine adds a further 9 points, and memory adds more. Selective memory beats full history (SR 56.0, avg 122.3 frames) and uniform keyframes (65.0) with only about 22 frames (67.0), so compactness beats volume. Memory also shrinks the drop caused by imperfect NVS (64→56 without memory vs 70→67 with it).
method: Where2Imagine: ResNet-18 trained from scratch on Habitat-Web human demonstrations (80k ObjectNav + 12k Pick&Place) to regress relative waypoint pose (dx, dy, dtheta) from an RGB view; data filtered by mean depth ≥0.3 and |dtheta|≤30°, MSE loss, horizon T=11.
Novel view synthesis: pretrained diffusion model PolyOculus renders the imagined observation at each predicted pose from each of the 6 panoramic views (60° apart), without fine-tuning.

Selective Foveation Memory: DINOv2 features, cosine-similarity segmentation of history, and the keyframe nearest the segment centroid; recent/medium/distant tiers use decreasing thresholds (0.8/0.73/0.6). An incremental O(1) streaming variant cuts update latency from 1.70 s to 0.16 s.

VLM planner: frozen GPT-4o-mini receives the goal, the 6 stitched imagined views with option labels, and the hierarchical memory, and returns JSON {Reason, Choice}; it is triggered every time a sub-goal is reached.
Low-level controller: VER-trained PointNav policy navigates to the chosen waypoint, turning goal-oriented navigation into a sequence of point-goal tasks.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o-mini (frozen) as planner; ResNet-18 (trained from scratch) Where2Imagine; PolyOculus (frozen) NVS; DINOv2 (frozen) memory; VER PointNav policy
setting.model_size: Where2Imagine ResNet-18 11.4M; VLM is API-based (open Qwen3-VL 2B-32B variants also tested)
setting.training_data: Where2Imagine trained on Habitat-Web human demonstrations (80k ObjectNav + 12k Pick&Place trajectories, MP3D); VLM and NVS are zero-shot, PointNav policy pretrained VER
setting.observation: egocentric panoramic RGB-D (6 views), no map
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: Stop, MoveAhead 25cm, Turn 30°, LookUp/Down, via PointNav sub-goals
setting.privileged: none (Oracle variant uses real images at predicted waypoints)

numbers.extra: mapless; Where2Imagine trained on human demos

numbers_note: Ablation runs use 100 episodes ("epochs"); main tables use 200. The split is not named explicitly, so 'val' is used. The Gibson entry is labeled other:Gibson-ObjNav because it is not a listed canonical benchmark.
results: On HM3D ObjectNav, mapless ImagineNav++ reaches 58.5 SR / 26.6 SPL, beating map-based VLFM (52.5) and UniGoal (54.5) in SR, and reaches 64.5 SR on HSSD vs ImagineNav 51.0. On instance-image navigation it reaches 52.4 SR and 32.8 SPL (best SPL; UniGoal has higher SR at 60.2). It trails VLFM on Gibson (72.4 vs 84.0 SR).
limitations: Performance is bounded by the quality of the off-the-shelf NVS model (hallucinated objects; a gap to the oracle of about 4-5 SR), and inference latency remains high.
Evaluated in simulation only, with the ablations on small 100-episode sets; the VLM planner relies on a paid closed API by default.
The simulator misses some target instances (false failures), and visually ambiguous targets cause recognition failures.
